title: Compose example multi-homes the whitelister and BunkerWeb on bw-universe without a fixed address, so proxied requests can arrive from a peer outside TRUSTED_PROXIES and collapse every client identity onto the proxy
description: docker-compose.example.yml (the file README.md:102 starts in the quick start) attaches the whitelister to bw-services (10.20.30.0/24) and bw-universe (10.20.40.0/24) and sketches BunkerWeb and bw-scheduler on the same two networks, but pins BunkerWeb only on bw-services (ipv4_address 10.20.30.2) and leaves its bw-universe address dynamic. .env.example sets TRUSTED_PROXIES=10.20.30.2/32 and LIST_ALLOWED_NETWORKS=10.20.30.0/24, i.e. only the bw-services side. Because the whitelister has an address on both networks, a lookup of `whitelister` from a container that shares both networks can resolve to its bw-universe address, so BunkerWeb's REVERSE_PROXY_HOST=http://whitelister:8080 or the scheduler's WHITELIST_IP_URLS download may connect over bw-universe from an unpinned 10.20.40.x source. Re-derived in the sandbox (app built from TRUSTED_PROXIES=10.20.30.2/32, LIST_ALLOWED_NETWORKS=10.20.30.0/24, dummy secrets, no BW_API_URL): security.py:254-255 returns (peer, False) for peer 10.20.40.3, so GET /login renders 10.20.40.3 as the visitor while peer 10.20.30.2 renders the forwarded 203.0.113.5; three wrong passwords from three different forwarded clients via peer 10.20.40.3 lock the shared key and the fourth client gets 429, whereas via the trusted peer each client keeps its own key (401 x4); POST /i/<token> via peer 10.20.40.3 whitelists 10.20.40.3 (accepted because ALLOW_PRIVATE=yes in .env.example) and records it as the invite's address instead of 203.0.113.5; GET /ips.txt with the correct token returns 200 from 10.20.30.9 and 403 from 10.20.40.9. Identity spoofing stays impossible (fail-closed), but whenever the bw-universe path is chosen: any anonymous visitor can lock the login and invite throttles for everyone (LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES=3, within the 6r/m /login limit), audit/history actors become the proxy's internal address, invitation redemption and add=me grant the proxy's internal address instead of the visitor's (the invitee receives no access), and the scheduler's list download is refused so the list goes stale. Whether Docker's embedded DNS and BunkerWeb 1.6.17's nginx actually route proxy or scheduler traffic over bw-universe, and whether the owner's real stack keeps this attachment (the compose file itself says the BunkerWeb services are only sketched, lines 2 and 45), is not visible in source.
claimed_root_cause: docker-compose.example.yml:18-20 attaches the whitelister to bw-universe as well as bw-services, and docker-compose.example.yml:50-53 pins BunkerWeb's address only on bw-services while leaving it unpinned on bw-universe (line 51); .env.example:15 and :24 therefore name only the bw-services address/subnet, so any proxy or scheduler connection that Docker's multi-network name resolution sends over bw-universe arrives from a peer that config.py:204 / security.py:254 do not recognise as the ingress.

trace.description: The whitelister joins bw-universe in addition to bw-services (line 19), so its name resolves to an address on each network for containers that share both; no ports are published.

BunkerWeb also joins bw-universe but only bw-services carries ipv4_address: 10.20.30.2 (line 53); its bw-universe address is dynamic. bw-scheduler (lines 62-64) shares both networks too, unpinned on both.
TRUSTED_PROXIES=10.20.30.2/32 names only the bw-services address; LIST_ALLOWED_NETWORKS=10.20.30.0/24 (line 24) likewise excludes bw-universe.

The value becomes settings.trusted_proxies, the only network tuple consulted for every identity decision (app.py:167-169 is the single resolver; uvicorn proxy_headers=False, forwarded_allow_ips=[] in __main__.py:29-30).

A peer outside trusted_proxies returns (peer_ip, False): the forwarding header from the real ingress is discarded and the proxy's internal 10.20.40.x address becomes the client identity (re-verified in-sandbox for peer 10.20.40.3: (10.20.40.3, False); peer 10.20.30.2: (203.0.113.5, True)).

throttle_key(parse_ip(ip)) is derived from that collapsed address, so all proxied clients share one login lock key (in-sandbox: 3 failures from 3 forwarded clients via peer 10.20.40.3, 4th client 429; via 10.20.30.2 all 401). open_invite at line 685 keys the invite throttle the same way.

store.upsert(net, ...) with net = redeemer_network(ip) (line 733) writes the proxy's internal address to the whitelist under the invitee's name instead of the invitee's address (in-sandbox: active_networks ['10.20.40.3'] via the unpinned peer, ['203.0.113.5'] via the pinned one); the same identity feeds created_by (line 548), events.actor (line 245) and the JSON audit log (line 313).

evidence.description: whitelister networks list: bw-services (commented: reachable by bunkerweb and bw-scheduler) and bw-universe (line 20, commented: reachable to bw-api); no `ports:` published.
Comment states the intent that TRUSTED_PROXIES name the ingress alone via the fixed address; the pin at line 53 covers only bw-services, line 51 leaves bw-universe unpinned.
bw-scheduler is attached to bw-universe and bw-services, so its list download may also leave over bw-universe, where LIST_ALLOWED_NETWORKS rejects it.
The BunkerWeb-side services are declared abbreviated/sketched (also line 2), so the real attachment of bunkerweb and bw-scheduler in the owner's stack is not fixed by this file.
TRUSTED_PROXIES=10.20.30.2/32.
LIST_ALLOWED_NETWORKS=10.20.30.0/24.
ALLOW_PRIVATE=yes, so parse_network accepts the proxy's private 10.20.40.x address when an invite redemption or add=me submits it.

`if not trusted_proxies or not in_networks(peer_ip, trusted_proxies): return peer_ip, False` - forwarded identity dropped for unrecognised peers (fail-closed against spoofing, but collapses identity onto the peer).
/ips.txt refuses peers outside list_allowed_networks; in-sandbox peer 10.20.40.9 with the correct token received 403, peer 10.20.30.9 received 200.
Quick start runs `docker compose -f docker-compose.example.yml up -d whitelister`, making the whitelister's network attachment in this file the maintained deployment path.

title: Prefill query values (over-long label, non-decimal Unicode digit days) raise unhandled exceptions out of GET /, producing a header-less 500 that an anonymous next-link can make the operator's post-login landing page
description: The logged-in index page pre-fills the add form from /?add=&days=&label=. Only the add value is guarded: a label that is still longer than 64 characters after normalisation makes normalize_label raise ValidationError, and a days value made of Unicode digit characters that are not decimal digits (e.g. U+00B2 SUPERSCRIPT TWO) passes the str.isdigit() guard but makes int() raise ValueError. index() does not catch either, the app registers no exception handler for ValueError/ValidationError, so the exception propagates through SecurityHeadersMiddleware.dispatch before any header is set and Starlette's outermost ServerErrorMiddleware answers a bare 500 'Internal Server Error' (no Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options or Cache-Control: no-store) and re-raises so the server logs a traceback. Because the anonymous branch of index forwards any query string into /login?next= and safe_next accepts any local path of up to 512 characters, an anonymous party can hand the operator a link whose post-login landing page is this 500 instead of the prefilled form. The same unguarded normalize_label call exists in POST /invites (name), but it is only reachable by the operator (session + CSRF + same-origin via require_post). The effect is confined to the single request: the process keeps serving, no entry or invite is written, and the prefill 'never writes anything' guarantee holds. Independently reproduced in a sandboxed in-process harness against the pinned FastAPI 0.162 / Starlette 1.10 / httpx 0.28 stack.
root_cause: prefill_from_query (whitelister/app.py:253-267) wraps only network_text(parse_network(...)) in try/except ValidationError (lines 260-263). Line 265 guards int(q['days']) with str.isdigit(), which is True for Unicode digit characters such as U+00B2 that are not decimal digits and that int() rejects with ValueError (str.isdecimal() or str.isascii() would be the correct guard). Line 267 calls normalize_label(q.get('label', '')) outside any try, and normalize_label raises ValidationError('error.label_too_long') when the normalised text exceeds MAX_LABEL=64 (whitelister/entries.py:34-35). index() calls prefill_from_query at app.py:492 with no exception handling, and the FastAPI app created at app.py:148 registers no exception handler (FastAPI's defaults cover only HTTPException and RequestValidationError), so both exceptions leave the route, cross SecurityHeadersMiddleware.dispatch at app.py:87 before the headers are added, and are turned into a bare 500 by Starlette's ServerErrorMiddleware. create_invite (app.py:635) repeats the unguarded normalize_label(name) call before its try block at 638.
intended_behavior: Prefill is best-effort and must never fail the page: an invalid or over-long value should fall back to the default (as the add value already does at lines 262-263) or be reported through the flash mechanism, and the index page must always render through SecurityHeadersMiddleware with its headers. Operator form validation errors in create_invite should become a flash via redirect_with_flash, as add_entry does for ValidationError.

trace.description: Anonymous GET / with any query string: lines 474-478 answer 303 to '/login?next=' + quote('/?' + request.url.query), carrying attacker-chosen label/days values unchanged.
Accepts any local path (starts with '/', not '//', no backslash, length <= 512); the crafted query survives, and login.html:12 echoes it as the hidden next field.
After a correct password the operator is redirected (303) to safe_next(next_url), i.e. to the crafted /?add=me&label=... or /?add=me&days=... URL.
'prefill': prefill_from_query(request, ip) is evaluated inside the context dict with no try/except.
q.get('days', '').isdigit() is True for U+00B2 (isdecimal() is False) but int(q['days']) raises ValueError.
normalize_label(q.get('label', '')) is called in the return expression, outside the try that protects parse_network.
Raises ValidationError('error.label_too_long', max=64) when the NFC/whitespace/control-normalised text is longer than 64 characters.

The exception leaves 'response = await call_next(request)' before any header is set; no app exception handler exists, so Starlette's ServerErrorMiddleware returns a bare 500 'Internal Server Error' without CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options or Cache-Control: no-store, and re-raises for the server log.

evidence.description: try/except ValidationError covers only network_text(parse_network(...)) (lines 260-263); the days and label handling below it is unprotected.
if q.get('days', '').isdigit() and int(q['days']) in settings.duration_presets: isdigit() accepts Unicode digit characters (U+00B2, U+00B3, U+2460...) that int() rejects.
return {..., 'label': normalize_label(q.get('label', ''))} with no exception handling.
'prefill': prefill_from_query(request, ip) inside index() with no try/except.
Anonymous branch of index forwards the whole query string into /login?next=quote('/?' + query).
login() redirects to safe_next(next_url) after a correct password, so the crafted path becomes the post-login landing page.
create_invite: clean_name = normalize_label(name) runs before the try block at 638, so a >64-char name raises out of the handler (operator-only, behind require_post).
normalize_label raises ValidationError('error.label_too_long') when len(text) > MAX_LABEL (64); ValidationError subclasses ValueError.
FastAPI app is created here; no app.exception_handler / add_exception_handler appears anywhere under whitelister/ (grep), so ValueError/ValidationError become a bare 500.
The label input has maxlength=64 (invite name at line 191 likewise), so the over-length branch is reachable only via a crafted URL or request, not the rendered form.
The login form carries the next value as a hidden input, so the crafted destination survives the login round-trip.
test_prefill_link_survives_login_and_only_prefills exercises only days=7, label=Laptop and a policy-violating add value; no over-long label or non-decimal digit days case.

conditions.description: The failing render happens in an operator session (logged in). The crafted URL can be produced and delivered by an anonymous party; an unauthenticated GET of it only yields the 303 to /login?next=... (verified: the 303 carries the security headers).
The operator must open the crafted link (and log in from it if not yet logged in) or hand-edit the URL / invite POST themselves; the rendered form cannot produce the input because of maxlength=64.
No stored state is required or changed; the effect is one failed response per crafted request and the app keeps serving.

execution.attacker_perspective: An anonymous party who can get the operator to click a link to the whitelister (e.g. in a message asking for an address to be listed) can make the operator's post-login landing page a bare 500 instead of the prefilled form; the operator recovers by visiting / again. The operator can also trigger it themselves with a hand-edited URL or a crafted POST /invites.
payloads: GET /login?next=%2F%3Fadd%3Dme%26label%3Daaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa  (what the anonymous 303 produces; the operator logs in from here)
instructions: Build the app in-process as tests/conftest.py does: load_settings() with dummy env (WHITELISTER_PASSWORD, SESSION_SECRET, DATA_DIR in a writable scratch dir, COOKIE_SECURE=no, TRUSTED_PROXIES=10.0.0.0/8, BW_API_URL/USERNAME/PASSWORD, WHITELIST_URL, SYNC_DEBOUNCE_SECONDS=0, TZ=UTC), EntryStore(':memory:'), BunkerWebClient whose _client uses an httpx.MockTransport fake bw-api, and httpx.AsyncClient over httpx.ASGITransport(app, client=('10.0.0.5', 40000), raise_app_exceptions=False) with header X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.9.

POST /login with the dummy password (303 to /); GET /?add=me&days=7&label=Laptop and record status 200 and the Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, Cache-Control and X-Content-Type-Options headers (baseline); GET /?add=me&label=<64 x 'a'> as the boundary control (expect 200).

In the same logged-in client GET /?add=me&label=<65 x 'a'> and GET /?add=me&days=%C2%B2; record status and which of the four headers are present. GET /?add=me&days=%D9%A7 (U+0667) as a control (expect 200 with dur-7 checked).
Repeat the two failing GETs with raise_app_exceptions=True to capture the exception type and the whitelister frames of the traceback.

Anonymous chain on a fresh app: without a session GET /?add=me&label=<65 x 'a'> (expect 303 to /login?next=...), GET that login page and confirm the hidden next field echoes the path, POST /login with password and next=<crafted path> (expect 303 to the crafted path), then GET that location.
Operator variant: GET / for a CSRF token, POST /invites (Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site same-origin) with name of 65 characters and otherwise valid fields; then with 64 characters as the boundary control.
Confirm GET / afterwards is 200 with headers and store.count() == 0 (no state effect); check safe_next with a 512- and a 513-character next to confirm the length gate.
execution.observed_result: Primitives: normalize_label('a'*65) raised ValidationError key=error.label_too_long params={'max': 64} (isinstance ValueError True); normalize_label('a'*64) accepted; '\u00b2'.isdigit()=True, isdecimal()=False, int('\u00b2') -> ValueError "invalid literal for int() with base 10: '²'"; '\u0667'.isdigit()=True and int()=7; duration_presets=(1, 7, 14, 30). Logged in: GET /?add=me&days=7&label=Laptop -> 200 with all four headers, value="203.0.113.9", dur-7 checked, value="Laptop". GET /?add=me&label=<64 a> -> 200 with headers. GET /?add=me&label=<65 a> -> 500 body 'Internal Server Error', all four headers absent. GET /?add=me&days=%C2%B2 -> 500, headers absent. GET /?add=me&days=%D9%A7 -> 200 with headers, dur-7 checked. GET / afterwards -> 200 with headers, store.count()=0. With raise_app_exceptions=True: whitelister.entries.ValidationError: error.label_too_long with frames app.py:87 dispatch -> app.py:492 index -> app.py:267 prefill_from_query -> entries.py:35 normalize_label; builtins.ValueError invalid literal for int() with frames app.py:87 dispatch -> app.py:492 index -> app.py:265 prefill_from_query. Anonymous chain on a fresh app: anon GET crafted -> 303 Location /login?next=%2F%3Fadd%3Dme%26label%3Daaa... (headers present); login page echoes next; POST /login with next -> 303 to the crafted path; GET that location -> 500 'Internal Server Error' without the four headers; GET / afterwards 200, store.count()=0; an anonymous GET of either crafted URL without a session is only the 303 (no pre-auth 500). Operator variant: POST /invites name=<65 n> with valid CSRF -> 500 without headers, invites_open=0; name=<64 n> -> 303 to /, invites_open=1. safe_next: a 512-char next is returned verbatim, 513 chars falls back to '/'.

remediation.strategy: Make prefill best-effort for all three values so prefill_from_query can never raise: guard the days parse with str.isdecimal()/isascii() (or try/except ValueError) and fall back to None, and catch ValidationError from normalize_label (fall back to an empty label). Move create_invite's normalize_label into a try and flash the ValidationError via redirect_with_flash like add_entry does. Optionally register a catch-all exception handler so that any future unhandled error still passes through SecurityHeadersMiddleware. Add regression tests for a 65-character label, days=%C2%B2 and a 65-character invite name expecting 200/303 with the security headers.

likelihood.reason: Requires the operator to open a crafted link (or craft the URL/request themselves); the rendered form cannot produce the input because of maxlength=64. The anonymous delivery path via /login?next= is straightforward but interaction-dependent, and only the operator session ever reaches the failing code.

impact.reason: One request fails with a bare 500 that lacks the security headers (static plaintext body, so the missing headers are inert) and an unhandled traceback is logged; the process keeps serving, no entry or invite is written, and the operator recovers by loading / again. No confidentiality or integrity effect; borders on informational and is a robustness defect in an anonymous-reachable input path rather than an exploitable weakness.

confidence.reason: Every trace line was re-read in source at 4ce6e0d and both branches were independently reproduced in a sandboxed in-process harness against the pinned dependencies (Starlette 1.10.0, FastAPI 0.162.0, httpx 0.28.1) with exception types and whitelister frames captured; the anonymous next-link chain and the operator /invites variant were reproduced end to end, and the boundary controls (64 chars, U+0667, 512/513-char next) behave as the source predicts.

title: Unlimited free invite renewals let a link holder trigger one BunkerWeb cache-delete/refresh per request and wipe the operator's on-page history
description: POST /i/{token} from an address that already redeemed the link is free by design (README.md:219-220) and the invite throttle only counts failed lookups (app.py:688-695: retry_after honours locks set by record_failure; a valid token calls record_success). Every such POST nevertheless runs the full change path: it rewrites the entry (app.py:741), appends an 'invite_refresh' event that evicts older rows beyond the 200-row cap (app.py:746, entries.py:307) and awaits refresh_after_change -> BunkerWebClient.trigger_refresh immediately (app.py:747, 316-325), bypassing SYNC_DEBOUNCE_SECONDS, which only applies in Syncer._run (bunkerweb.py:224-225). The active network set does not change (the address is already listed), so each refresh is a pure cost: a DELETE /cache/global/whitelist/whitelist-download/<sha1>.list (POST /jobs/run on 404) that, per the client's own documentation, makes the scheduler re-run the whitelist job, regenerate the configuration and reload. A plain HTTP client works because same_origin (app.py:221-232) passes requests without Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site. Verified in the sandbox with SYNC_DEBOUNCE_SECONDS=3: 250 renewals from one known address -> 250 HTTP 200, 250 outbound DELETE calls, active list unchanged, events table 200 rows all invite_refresh, the operator's 4 history rows gone, budget still 1 of 3.
root_cause: invite_redeem (app.py:725-751) treats a renewal of an already-active address like a list change: it unconditionally calls store.event_add and refresh_after_change (app.py:746-747); the request-time refresh path (app.py:316-325, bunkerweb.py:115-134) has no debounce or rate limit (the debounce lives only in Syncer._run, bunkerweb.py:224-225); and successful redemptions are never throttled or budgeted (open_invite records only failures, app.py:688-695; the known-address branch skips the budget check, app.py:736-738).
intended_behavior: Renewals from a known address should be a cheap, bounded operation: the operator-owned integration (bw-api calls, BunkerWeb reloads) and the on-page history should be touched only when the published list actually changes, and a lower-trust link holder should not be able to drive them at request rate.

trace.description: POST /i/{token} is reachable without a session; same_origin (221-232) accepts clients that send neither Origin nor Sec-Fetch-Site.
A valid, open token calls invite_throttle.record_success; only unknown/closed tokens count as failures (692), so successful POSTs are unlimited.
known = address already in invite_addresses: the budget check at 737-738 is skipped and the renewal costs nothing.
store.event_add('invite_refresh', ...) on every renewal; entries.py:307 deletes all rows beyond the newest 200, evicting operator history.
refresh_after_change is awaited unconditionally, even though the active network set is unchanged.
client.trigger_refresh() is called directly; the debounce (bunkerweb.py:224-225, SYNC_DEBOUNCE_SECONDS) exists only in Syncer._run.

DELETE /cache/global/whitelist/whitelist-download/<sha1>.list per request (POST /jobs/run on 404): per the module docstring (lines 3-8) each one makes the scheduler re-download the list, regenerate the configuration and reload the instances.

evidence.description: retry_after only blocks after recorded failures (security.py:158-167 reads locks set by record_failure); no limiter covers successful redemptions.
'if not known and invite.remaining == 0' - a known address never consumes budget, so renewals are unlimited.
'sync_error = await refresh_after_change(request)' runs for renewals that change nothing in the published list.
event_add trims the events table to the newest 200 rows (_MAX_EVENTS, line 18), so 200 renewals remove every operator row.
The only sleep(sync_debounce_seconds) is in Syncer._run; trigger_refresh (115-130) called from the request path has none.
SYNC_DEBOUNCE_SECONDS is documented as 'Collect quick successive changes before one refresh', which the direct path does not honour.
The example bw-api deployment sets 'API_RATE_LIMIT_RULES=DELETE /cache* 30r/m', which bounds the downstream cost in that deployment (excess deletes become errors shown in the operator header).
The only renewal test performs a single second click; repeated renewals and their outbound call count are untested.

conditions.description: Possession of an open invitation link (no password or session); the first POST from the address consumes one budget slot, every later one from that address is free.
BW_API_URL and WHITELIST_URL configured (otherwise refresh_after_change / trigger_refresh return early and only the history eviction remains).

The cost on the BunkerWeb side (job re-run, configuration regeneration, instance reload per cache delete) is taken from the client's own documentation and was not observed locally; the compose example's 'DELETE /cache* 30r/m' limit would turn the excess into non-2xx responses surfaced as an API error to the operator.

execution.attacker_perspective: Anyone holding an invitation link, after one normal redemption, repeats POST /i/<token> from the same address with a plain HTTP client (no cookies, no Origin or Sec-Fetch-Site headers).
payloads: POST /i/<token> HTTP/1.1 (no body, no cookies, no Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site) repeated 250 times from an address that already redeemed the link
check_renewals.py (sandbox): operator login -> 3 entries -> POST /invites name=Tax advisor access_days=7 link_days=14 max_addresses=3 -> guest 203.0.113.77 POST /i/<token> once, then 250 more times
instructions: Build the app in-process as tests/conftest.py does: EntryStore(':memory:'), BunkerWebClient whose httpx client is an httpx.MockTransport that records calls and answers 200 to DELETE /cache/..., with env WHITELISTER_PASSWORD, SESSION_SECRET (40 chars), TRUSTED_PROXIES=10.0.0.0/8, COOKIE_SECURE=no, BW_API_URL=http://bw-api:8888, BW_API_USERNAME/BW_API_PASSWORD dummies, WHITELIST_URL=http://whitelister:8080/ips.txt, SYNC_DEBOUNCE_SECONDS=3, TZ=UTC.

As the operator (ASGI peer 10.0.0.5, X-Forwarded-For 203.0.113.1) log in, add three entries (POST /entries with duration=7), create an invite (POST /invites) and read the token from the link shown on the page.
As a guest (peer 10.0.0.5, X-Forwarded-For 203.0.113.77, no Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site) POST /i/<token> once, then 250 more times; record each status.

title: Invitation redemption grants the creation-time access_days without re-applying the current MAX_DAYS policy
description: The candidate claims that after the operator lowers MAX_DAYS, POST /i/{token} lets a link holder (no operator password) put their address on the whitelist for the invite's stored access_days, i.e. 'longer than the current configuration permits anyone to grant', that the operator could not grant that period themselves, and that the stale authorisation is invisible. The mechanics are real and were reproduced (redemption under MAX_DAYS=30 of a link created with access_days=365 stored an entry expiring 364 days ahead), but the security framing is refuted by source and by the same local run: MAX_DAYS is not a ceiling on what may be on the list (the operator grants unlimited 'forever' access through add, extend and import under any MAX_DAYS), the duration is exactly the grant the operator made for that link, the open invite with its 365-day period is listed on the operator dashboard next to a Revoke button, and stored entries with expiries beyond the new MAX_DAYS are likewise neither trimmed nor warned about at startup. No lower-trust principal obtains anything beyond what the operator explicitly authorised.
claimed_root_cause: whitelister/app.py invite_redeem (app.py:739) uses invite.access_days, the copy of the operator's choice stored at creation (app.py:640-641, entries.py:355-358), as the duration passed to EntryStore.upsert (entries.py:237-255), which enforces no duration policy; neither open_invite/is_open (entries.py:122-123) nor policy_violations at startup (entries.py:466-474, app.py:133) re-validates stored invites against settings.max_days, whereas add (entries.py:69-72), extend (app.py:586-589), import (app.py:841-842) and invite creation (app.py:640) check the live settings.max_days.

trace.description: Operator posts access_days; it is validated once against settings.max_days as of that moment (lines 640-641) and stored verbatim in invites.access_days via store.invite_create (line 653).
access_days persisted as an INTEGER column with no further relation to settings; it survives restarts and configuration changes.

Link holder POSTs /i/{token}; open_invite (lines 682-696) checks token hash, throttle, revoked_at and valid_until (Invite.is_open, entries.py:122-123); access_days is not compared with the current policy.
expires = now + timedelta(days=invite.access_days) taken from the stored copy; no min(..., settings.max_days) and no expiry_from_days call.
The expires_at is written to entries (or replaces an existing row's expiry); active_networks (entries.py:291-297) then serves the address in /ips.txt for the stored period.

evidence.description: expires = now + timedelta(days=invite.access_days): the stored value is used as-is (verified; this part of the candidate holds).

if not 1 <= days <= settings.max_days: raise ValueError in create_invite: the operator chose and was bound by MAX_DAYS when the grant was made; the redeemed duration is this operator decision, not a link-holder choice.

parse_duration: if duration == 'forever': return None. Under any MAX_DAYS the operator adds entries that never expire (sandbox: POST /entries duration=forever under MAX_DAYS=30 stored expires_at=None), so MAX_DAYS does not bound what may be on the list and the claim 'longer than the current configuration permits anyone to grant' is false.

extend_entry: if duration == 'forever': new_end = None. The same 365-day row the candidate says cannot be extended by 365 days is extended to unlimited under MAX_DAYS=30 (sandbox: expires_at became None), so the cited sibling path does not establish a duration ceiling either.
_parse_import_expiry: null/empty expiry returns None (never expires); the import 'ceiling' at line 841 only bounds finite ISO dates.

Operator dashboard renders every open invite with t('invite.summary', access=<access_days> ...) ('{access} access per address · link until {until}', en.json:152) and a Revoke form (line 220). Sandbox: after the restart the page contained '365 days access per address' and /invites/1/revoke, so the stale period is not invisible.

The cited contract reads 'a row accepted under an earlier, looser MIN_PREFIX_*/ALLOW_PRIVATE cannot be revived or made permanent once the policy is tightened; such rows are warned about at startup': it is about network policy, not MAX_DAYS, and matches policy_violations (entries.py:466-474), which only calls parse_network.

MAX_DAYS is documented only as 'Longest allowed duration' (an input bound next to DURATION_PRESETS); no documented or source-visible guarantee says lowering it shortens or disables grants made earlier.

policy_violations ignores duration entirely: a 365-day operator entry created before the restart was neither trimmed nor warned about under MAX_DAYS=30 in the sandbox (0 rows flagged, lifespan logged no stale-policy warning). Stored invites behave exactly like stored entries: the grant stands as made.

reason: Refuted as a vulnerability; the behaviour is a documented-grant-stands-as-made lifecycle, not stale authorisation crossing a trust boundary. (1) No unauthorised mutation: the link holder receives exactly the access_days the operator chose for that link under the MAX_DAYS in force at the time (app.py:640-653); they cannot influence the duration. (2) MAX_DAYS is not a ceiling on what may be whitelisted: under MAX_DAYS=30 the operator still grants unlimited access via add 'forever' (app.py:372), extend 'forever' (app.py:577) and import null expiry (app.py:832-833); the sandbox run (check-1-v3-9-redeem-max-days.txt, exit 0) stored expires_at=None through add and extend under MAX_DAYS=30, so the statements 'longer than the current configuration permits anyone to grant' and 'the operator could not grant that period themselves' are false. (3) The intended-behaviour source README.md:81-83 concerns MIN_PREFIX_*/ALLOW_PRIVATE network policy; policy_violations (entries.py:466-474) checks parse_network only, and a 365-day entry created before the restart was likewise left untouched and unwarned (0 rows flagged, no lifespan warning), so invites are consistent with how every other stored grant is treated, not an outlier. (4) Not invisible: index.html:219-220 lists each open invite with '<N> days access per address' and a Revoke button; the sandbox page after the restart showed '365 days access per address' and the revoke form, and revocation is a one-click operator action. The hunter's own observation (redemption stores now+365d under MAX_DAYS=30) was reproduced and is accurate, but under DATA-ISOLATION-AND-LIFECYCLE validation rules 1-2 there is no unauthorised reader/mutation and no source-of-truth policy that the redeem path disagrees with. Capping redemptions at the live MAX_DAYS (or listing over-policy invites in the startup log) remains a reasonable consistency hardening for the owner, at informational level, not a finding. Sandbox details: two create_app instances over one SQLite file via ASGITransport with a fake bw-api MockTransport, TEST-NET addresses only; 60 s / 1 GiB / loopback-only runner; verdicts all true, exit 0.

title: Invite redemption silently shortens and re-attributes an operator-managed whitelist entry for the same network
description: POST /i/{token} writes the redeemer's network through EntryStore.upsert without checking whether an entry for that network already exists. upsert's ON CONFLICT(network) clause replaces expires_at and created_by unconditionally and replaces label whenever the new label is non-empty (invite names are required). A link holder who connects from a network the operator already whitelisted (a bare IPv4 address, or exactly the /64 for IPv6, e.g. an office NAT address listed 'forever') therefore converts the operator's grant into a short invite grant of invite.access_days, relabels it with the invite name and re-attributes it to 'invite:<name>'. GET /i/{token} derives 'known' only from this invite's invite_addresses, so such an address is shown as 'ready' and neither party is warned. When the shortened period ends the whole network drops off the list. The store keeps no copy of the previous row; the original label survives only in the 200-row on-page history ('add' event) until evicted and the original expiry only in the stderr audit log. A lower-trust principal (link holder) thereby mutates operator-owned state beyond the invite's documented authority of adding or renewing their own access.
root_cause: whitelister/app.py:736 computes known only from store.invite_addresses(invite.id), never from store.find(net); app.py:739-741 then computes expires = now + access_days and calls store.upsert(net, invite.name, expires, now, created_by='invite:<name>') for any redeemer network; whitelister/entries.py:246-250 (ON CONFLICT(network) DO UPDATE SET label = CASE WHEN excluded.label = '' THEN entries.label ELSE excluded.label END, expires_at = excluded.expires_at, created_by = excluded.created_by) replaces the existing row with no ownership, expiry or attribution check anywhere on the path.
intended_behavior: Per README.md:215-221 and locales/en.json invite.admin_text, a link lets a person 'put their own address on the list for the access period' and opening it from a known address 'only restarts that address's period'. An existing, longer or endless operator grant for the same network should be left intact (or at most extended) with its label and attribution preserved, and the page should present such an address as already unlocked.

trace.description: POST /i/{token} from an unauthenticated link holder; passes same_origin (726) and open_invite (728) with a valid open token.

The redeemer network is derived from the resolved client address (bare IPv4 or the IPv6 /64) via network_text(parse_network(...)) (app.py:275-284), the same textual form POST /entries stores, so it collides with an operator entry for the same network.
known is computed only from this invite's invite_addresses; an operator-created entry for the same network does not make the address known and no store.find(net) lookup happens.
store.upsert(net, invite.name, now + access_days, now, created_by='invite:<name>') is called regardless of an existing row for net.
ON CONFLICT(network) DO UPDATE replaces label (invite name is always non-empty), expires_at (shortening forever/long grants to access_days) and created_by of the operator's entry.

evidence.description: expires = now + timedelta(days=invite.access_days): the invite period is applied even when a longer or endless grant exists for the network.
entry = store.upsert(net, invite.name, expires, now, created_by=f"invite:{invite.name}") with no lookup of an existing entry for net.
expires_at = excluded.expires_at: the stored expiry is overwritten unconditionally on conflict.
label = CASE WHEN excluded.label = '' THEN entries.label ELSE excluded.label END: the operator label is replaced because invite names are required (app.py:636-637).
created_by = excluded.created_by: the operator's attribution is replaced by 'invite:<name>'.
GET /i/{token} renders 'known' (with the existing expiry) only when the address is in invite_addresses; an already-whitelisted operator network is shown as 'ready' with no warning.
Documented semantics: opening the link again from a known address 'only restarts that address's period'; nothing states that an operator's existing grant for the network is replaced.
The invite tests only redeem onto networks with no prior entry (store.count() == 0 before the first POST); no test covers redemption over a pre-existing operator entry.

conditions.description: The lower-trust principal holds an open invitation link (anyone the operator sent it to, or anyone it was forwarded to); no login is needed.

The whitelist already contains an operator-managed entry whose network text equals the redeemer's mapped network (bare IPv4 address, or exactly the /64 for IPv6), e.g. an office NAT address listed 'forever' or for 365 days.
The link holder connects from that network, e.g. the operator testing their own link from the whitelisted office, or a colleague/contractor opening a shared link from an already whitelisted site.

execution.attacker_perspective: A link holder (or the operator testing a link) connects from an address the operator has already whitelisted permanently, opens the link (page says 'Press the button and this connection is unlocked for 14 days', not 'already unlocked') and presses the button. The permanent grant becomes a 14-day grant labelled with the invite name and attributed to 'invite:<name>'; when it lapses, the whole network loses its whitelisting.

If one exists, is not expired and its expiry is later than (or endless compared to) now + access_days, keep it: record the touch so the address counts as known for this link, do not change expires_at, label or created_by, and render the 'known' state with the existing expiry. No tooling: one button press, and the page gives no hint.

title: /ips.txt 'direct request' gate is a fixed five-header denylist that neither refuses TRUSTED_PROXIES peers nor treats the configured CLIENT_IP_HEADER as proxy metadata
description: GET /ips.txt (whitelister/app.py:404-415) serves the full active whitelist when the TCP peer parses, is inside LIST_ALLOWED_NETWORKS, the optional LIST_TOKEN matches, and none of exactly five lowercase header names (x-forwarded-for, forwarded, x-real-ip, x-forwarded-host, x-forwarded-proto; whitelister/security.py:275-276) is present. The gate never consults settings.trusted_proxies or settings.client_ip_header. In the shipped topology the BunkerWeb ingress (10.20.30.2, TRUSTED_PROXIES=10.20.30.2/32) lies inside LIST_ALLOWED_NETWORKS=10.20.30.0/24 (and inside the default, all private ranges), and REVERSE_PROXY_URL=/ publishes every path including /ips.txt through that ingress. Reproduced in the sandbox (httpx.ASGITransport, dummy secrets, no network): with LIST_TOKEN unset, a request whose peer is the trusted-proxy address 10.20.30.2 with no header, or carrying only via / x-forwarded-port / cf-connecting-ip / true-client-ip / x-forwarded-server, returns 200 and the list (including with CLIENT_IP_HEADER=CF-Connecting-IP and only cf-connecting-ip present); the same peer with any of the five recognised names returns 403; an outsider peer 203.0.113.9 returns 403; with LIST_TOKEN set the right token is required and token plus x-forwarded-for is still 403. The app's documented design (README.md:70-73) relies on the proxy always adding one of those header names, so whether an anonymous internet client can reach the 200 state through the published UI origin depends on BunkerWeb 1.6.17's generated proxy_set_header lines and on REVERSE_PROXY_HEADERS / CDN deployment choices that are not in the repository, and on whether the deployed LIST_TOKEN is set.
claimed_root_cause: whitelister/security.py:275-276 implements the 'direct request' test as a denylist of five header names, and the gate at whitelister/app.py:410 does not additionally refuse peers inside settings.trusted_proxies (which never legitimately fetch the list; the scheduler does) nor treat settings.client_ip_header as a forwarding header, so the control depends on proxy header-insertion behaviour outside the application's own configuration rather than on the application's trust model.

title: Anonymous unknown-token requests from a handful of addresses lock every invitation link for all holders (shared process-wide throttle budget on /i/{token})
description: open_invite reuses LoginThrottle, including its process-wide budget of 30 failures per minute shared by all clients. Any anonymous client who can reach /i/ (which the README requires to be reachable without login) and who controls at least 11 throttle keys (IPv4 addresses or IPv6 /64 prefixes) can send 31 requests with made-up 20..64-character tokens within a minute; from then on open_invite answers 429 to every client, including legitimate holders of valid links, for both the GET page and the redeeming POST. Because a locked key is refused before it can add a failure, sustaining the lockout requires a growing pool of fresh keys (roughly 190 per hour) rather than the same 11; recovery is automatic 60 s after the attacker stops. The budget was designed to bound CPU spent on password hashing; for invite tokens the lookup is a SHA-256 plus an indexed SELECT and the 192-bit token cannot be guessed, so the global lock adds no protection here and only provides a denial lever against a security-relevant provisioning function.

title: Operator removal of an invite-created entry does not stick: the stale invite_addresses row lets the removed redeemer re-list itself past an exhausted budget, logged as a renewal
description: POST /entries/{entry_id}/delete removes only the `entries` row. The (invite_id, network) row that invite_touch_address wrote in `invite_addresses` for that redemption is left in place, and that row is the sole input to the `known` decision in invite_page/invite_redeem. While the link is still open, the anonymous holder of the link connecting from the address the operator just removed gets GET /i/{token} rendered in the 'known' state ('This connection is already unlocked until .' with an empty date, button 'Renew my access') and POST /i/{token} re-creates the entry for the full access period: the budget gate `if not known and invite.remaining == 0` is skipped (an exhausted link still admits the removed address while any other new address is refused with 409), invite_touch_address returns False, the audit event carries new_address=false and the on-page history says 'renewed via link'. The index keeps showing the address as consuming a slot of the invite ('1 of 1 addresses used') while it is not on the list. The operator's targeted removal therefore has no lasting effect against the removed guest unless the whole shared link is revoked. (By contrast, an entry that merely expired is documented to be renewable for free from the known address; the gap is specific to the operator's explicit delete.)
root_cause: Two tables describe one lifecycle fact. `entries` is the source of truth for 'is this network listed', while `invite_addresses` is a redemption history that invite_redeem (whitelister/app.py:736-738) treats as an authorization shortcut: known => skip the budget gate and classify the write as a refresh. EntryStore.delete (whitelister/entries.py:268-271) and delete_entry (whitelister/app.py:608-620) neither tombstone nor consult the redemption history, and invite_redeem never checks that a known address is actually still listed (store.find(net) is used only on the GET side for display, whitelister/app.py:721). invite_touch_address (whitelister/entries.py:392-404) then reports the re-add as not new because its UPDATE hits the stale row.
intended_behavior: README.md:218-220 and whitelister/locales/en.json:139 define the free re-redemption as 'opening it again from a known address is free and only restarts that address's period' / 'only refreshes that address', i.e. a renewal of an existing listing. An entry the operator removed through 'Remove {network} from the whitelist?' (en.json:69) has no period to restart: a later redemption from that address is either a new unlock that must pass the budget gate and be audited as new_address=true, or it is refused while the operator's removal stands. The operator-facing usage count should also not keep attributing a slot to an address that is no longer listed.

audit 'invite.redeem' with new_address=false (line 745) and history event 'invite_refresh'; the network is back in active_networks, the bw-api cache drop is issued and /ips.txt serves it again.

remediation.strategy: Make the redemption history agree with the entry lifecycle. When the operator deletes an entry, mark (do not delete, so the slot stays consumed) the matching invite_addresses rows as removed, and have invite_page/invite_redeem refuse a removed address while the removal stands (or, if re-admission is wanted, treat it as a new unlock: run the budget gate and make invite_touch_address report it as new). Do not derive `known` from invite_addresses alone: require store.find(net) to exist as well, otherwise the normal budget path and new_address=true audit apply. Note that only checking store.find is insufficient on its own because invite_touch_address's UPDATE would still hit the stale row and return False. Regression test: invite with max_addresses=1, redeem, operator delete, second GET from the same address must not render the 'already unlocked' state with an empty date, and a second POST must not re-create the entry (or must be counted and logged as a new unlock).
